(a) In General.—Not later than 180 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary of Defense shall implement a process for the expedited identification and replacement of obsolete electronic parts included in acquisition programs of the Department of Defense. 
    (b) Issues To Be Addressed.—At a minimum, the expedited process established pursuant to subsection (a) shall—
        (1) include a mechanism pursuant to which contractors, or other sources of supply, may provide to appropriate Department of Defense officials information that identifies—
            (A) obsolete electronic parts that are included in the specifications for an acquisition program of the Department of Defense; and 
            (B) suitable replacements for such electronic parts;  
        (2) specify timelines for the expedited review and validation of information submitted by contractors, or other sources of supply, pursuant to paragraph (1); 
        (3) specify procedures and timelines for the rapid submission and approval of engineering change proposals needed to accomplish the substitution of replacement parts that have been validated pursuant to paragraph (2); 
        (4) provide for any incentives for contractor participation in the expedited process that the Secretary may determine to be appropriate; and 
        (5) provide that, in addition to the responsibilities under section 2337 of title 10, United States Code, a product support manager for a major weapon system shall work to identify obsolete electronic parts that are included in the specifications for an aquisition program of the Department of Defense and approve suitable replacements for such electronic parts.  
    (c) Additional Matters.—For the purposes of this section—
        (1) an electronic part is obsolete if—
            (A) the part is no longer in production; and 
            (B) the original manufacturer of the part and its authorized dealers do not have sufficient parts in stock 
to meet the requirements of such an acquisition program; and  
        (2) an electronic part is a suitable replacement for an obsolete electronic part if—
            (A) the part could be substituted for an obsolete part without incurring unreasonable expense and without degrading system performance; and 
            (B) the part is or will be available in sufficient quantity to meet the requirements of such an acquisition program.

fable.w: The section requires the Secretary of Defense to set up a formal channel through which contractors and other suppliers, who are outside the federal government, submit information on obsolete parts and suitable replacements. The Department must then review and validate that information before deciding to approve substitutions, so outside input feeds a federal decision. The tempting contrary reading is that this is only contract administration or an application-like submission, but the contractors are not seeking a benefit here; they are supplying input the Department uses to decide. This is a close call because the process sits within procurement rather than policy-making.

opus.w: The Secretary must set up a mechanism that lets contractors and other suppliers, who are outside the federal government, give DoD information about obsolete parts and replacements. DoD then reviews, validates and approves substitutions based on that input, and the statute even allows incentives for 'contractor participation.' This is not an application for a contract or a defense against an agency finding. It is outside input into a federal decision about which parts to replace, so it counts as participation.

That reading fails. Contractors and other suppliers are outside the federal government. The statute sets up a channel for them to send the Department of Defense information that identifies obsolete parts and suitable replacements, and DoD then reviews that information and makes its own replacement decisions. They are not applying for anything or rebutting an accusation. They are giving input to a federal decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section establishes a mechanism for contractors to submit technical information (identifying obsolete parts and replacements) to the Department of Defense. This is a data submission process akin to providing quotes or specifications in a procurement context, not a consultation or coordination process where the government seeks advice or input from outside parties on a policy or decision. The contractors are not participating in the decision-making process itself, but rather providing inputs for the government's internal review. The mention of 'contractor participation' refers to their involvement in the data submission process, not in the governmental decision.

qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: The section mentions a "mechanism pursuant to which contractors... may provide... information" and "incentives for contractor participation." One might argue this constitutes participation because outside entities (contractors) are involved in the process of identifying obsolete parts. However, this is essentially a reporting or submission mechanism for technical data to facilitate an internal government procurement decision, not a consultation on policy or a grant of decision-making power to the outside party. The contractors are providing data to help the government make its own decision, similar to submitting an application or a report. The definition explicitly excludes "applications for benefits or grants" and notes that mere procedural interaction where the outside party is just providing information for an internal decision is not participation unless it involves consultation/coordination *before* a decision in a way that implies the outside party has a voice in the decision itself (like an advisory board or public comment period). Here, the contractors are just supplying data points. The "participation" mentioned in (b)(4) refers to contractors participating in the *process* of submitting data, not participating in the *decision* making. The key gate is whether the outside party is consulted/coordinates *before* a decision in a way that influences the decision through dialogue/advice, or if they are just submitting data. This looks more like data submission. However, looking closer at the definition: "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision." Does the government *consult* the contractors? It creates a mechanism for them to *provide information*. This is passive receipt of information, not active consultation. The government isn't asking for their opinion on a policy; it's asking for technical specs. This is akin to a vendor submitting a quote. Therefore, it is "No".

Wait, let's re-read the "No" traps. "applications for benefits, grants, contracts, or licenses - applying for something is not participating in the decision". This is similar. The contractors are providing info to get their parts approved. It's part of the procurement process.

Let's look at the "Yes" criteria: "consultation or coordination with states, tribes, local governments, or other outside entities before a federal action". Is providing a list of obsolete parts "consultation"? Usually, consultation implies a two-way dialogue or seeking advice. Here, the government is just setting up a channel to receive data.

Let's look at the "No" criteria again: "reports to, or notifications of, Congress...". This is not Congress. "consultation or coordination BETWEEN federal agencies...". This is not between agencies.

Is there any "advisory committee"? No.
Is there any "public comment period"? No.
Is there any "right to sue"? No.

The phrase "incentives for contractor participation" is boilerplate for encouraging them to use the new system. It doesn't change the nature of the interaction from data submission to decision-making participation.

Therefore, the label is "No".
